topics.label: Lecture introduction and aims
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic frames the lecture as an integration of previously introduced immune cells and molecules.

topics.label: Principles of innate immune recognition
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how innate immunity distinguishes danger through molecular patterns and appropriately positioned, germline-encoded receptors.

topics.label: Toll-like receptor recognition and signalling
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how Toll-like receptors translate microbial recognition into responses suited to the location of infection.

topics.label: Non-TLR recognition pathways and inflammatory disease
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how danger sensing through non-TLR pathways activates inflammation that can contribute to chronic disease.

topics.label: Sentinel-cell signalling and leukocyte recruitment
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how activated sentinel cells organise the inflammatory response, including the recruitment of circulating leukocytes to infected tissue.

topics.label: Lymphatic transport and adaptive immune priming
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how drainage from infected tissues enables dendritic cells to initiate adaptive immune responses in lymph nodes.

topics.label: Excessive systemic inflammation and septic shock
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic examines how excessive inflammatory activation becomes a life-threatening systemic response.

topics.label: Mechanisms that resolve inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how declining inflammatory stimuli and active inhibitory signals bring an immune response to an end.

topics.label: Tissue repair and persistent inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine recovery after inflammatory damage and why persistent triggers can require ongoing containment rather than complete restoration.

topics.label: Lecture close and next lecture
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic ends the lecture and identifies complement as the subject of the next lecture.
